tips.title: The system is read-only, on purpose.
tips.body: Bazzite's base install can't be casually broken. Apps install through Flatpak, sandboxed and separate from the parts that keep your system stable, instead of a package manager touching the core.

tips.title: There are three ways to install software, and when each one is right.
tips.body: Flatpak is the default for most apps, sandboxed and safe. Package layering, using rpm-ostree, can install almost anything traditional but requires a reboot every time and is best used sparingly. A container, using Distrobox, is best for developer tools that need a full traditional Linux environment running alongside Bazzite without touching the base system.

tips.title: Drag the file, skip the typing.
tips.body: Any terminal command that needs a file's location will accept a literal drag and drop. Pull the file from your file manager into the terminal window and the full path types itself, no memorizing paths required.

tips.title: The rollback screen on first real boot is normal.
tips.body: That's Bazzite's atomic update safety net showing itself, not a broken install.

tips.title: A blue setup screen asking to Enroll MOK is normal too.
tips.body: That's Secure Boot enrollment, a security key confirmation, not an error. It's part of a clean install, not a sign something went wrong.

tips.title: Everything on Linux needs the terminal is a skewed impression, not the reality.
tips.body: People making tutorials are disproportionately terminal-comfortable and default to typing out of habit even when a button does the same thing. Troubleshooting content is terminal-heavy because that's genuinely where interfaces fall short, but it overrepresents the worst case as if it were normal daily use. Day to day, most things have a button.

tips.title: Picking the wrong distro isn't the risk it feels like.
tips.body: Once something works, most people stay for years, not months. If you ever did switch, you're not starting from zero, you already understand what Linux is doing conceptually, you'd just be relearning some distro-specific vocabulary.

tips.title: BTRFS matters for your backup drive too, not just the system disk.
tips.body: Bazzite's own root filesystem uses BTRFS because it checksums data as it's written and can detect or self-heal corruption. Worth formatting an external backup drive the same way rather than defaulting to exFAT or NTFS.

tips.title: Built-in rollback already covers what a lot of people reach for a separate imaging tool for.
tips.body: A full disk imaging tool is really only useful as an occasional supplement before a risky change. Bazzite's atomic rollback already handles the an update broke something, restore a working state scenario most new users worry about.

tips.title: A website is often the simplest fix, not a fallback.
tips.body: Many services people assume need a dedicated app work perfectly as a website, and can be installed as a progressive web app, meaning a website that opens in its own window with its own icon and no browser toolbar, for a native feel without needing any dedicated Linux client at all.

tips.title: Verify Linux support before buying a niche peripheral.
tips.body: Some audio interfaces, capture cards, and specialty accessories need manual driver workarounds on Linux, or lack certain software controls, like gain knobs, entirely in software. A quick search for the exact model plus the word Linux before buying saves a real headache later.

tips.title: Plug and play hardware support is better than the old reputation suggests, though it's not universal.
tips.body: Webcams and most USB audio devices tend to just work with no driver hunting. It's a real improvement over Linux's old reputation, just not a guarantee for every device, see the peripheral tip above.

tips.title: Coming from ChromeOS, you already have more of a head start than it feels like.
tips.body: ChromeOS runs on a Linux kernel, but as a locked-down appliance where Google controls everything, no root access, no changing the desktop, no traditional installed software. Bazzite isn't introducing you to Linux so much as handing you the keys to something you were already halfway inside of. A lot of daily habits, Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Docs, all browser-based, keep working immediately with zero setup.

tips.title: There's more than one Bazzite edition, and picking the right one matters.
tips.body: A plain desktop edition for regular PCs and laptops, an edition that boots straight into a console-style Steam interface for handhelds and living-room setups, and a developer-focused edition are the main options. Most people setting up a regular desktop or laptop want the plain desktop edition.

tips.title: Your graphics drivers are already part of the operating system image, not something you install separately.
tips.body: AMD, Intel, and Nvidia drivers all come baked in and update automatically along with the rest of the system, there's no separate driver download to manage the way there is on Windows.

tips.title: Switching graphics card brands means switching your whole system image, not just installing a new driver.
tips.body: If you swap from an AMD or Intel card to an Nvidia one, or the other way around, you'll need to move to the matching image so the correct drivers are included.

tips.title: A message about a system transaction already in progress during an update isn't an error.
tips.body: It usually just means the system is already downloading and applying an update quietly in the background, safe to leave alone.

tips.title: Dual-booting with Windows can knock out your Wi-Fi or wired connection in Bazzite.
tips.body: Windows' Fast Startup feature leaves some hardware in a half-asleep state that can carry over strangely into Linux on the next boot. Turning Fast Startup off in Windows' power settings usually fixes it for good.

tips.title: If installing Windows afterward breaks your ability to boot into Bazzite, there's an official fix for that.
tips.body: A bootloader restoration tool, run from the same USB drive used to install Bazzite, can restore it without needing to reinstall anything.

tips.title: Switching your desktop environment later isn't as simple as flipping a setting.
tips.body: Moving from KDE to GNOME, or back, on an existing install tends to leave behind broken, mismatched configuration files. A fresh install of the other edition is the more reliable way to try it.

tips.title: Don't theme your bootloader.
tips.body: Customizing GRUB's appearance isn't supported and carries a real risk of leaving the system unable to boot at all.

tips.title: ujust commands turn common maintenance tasks into short, memorable phrases instead of long technical procedures.
tips.body: Typing ujust on its own lists everything available, things like updating everything at once, fixing crackling audio, or resetting Steam back to a clean state. A graphical app called Bazzite Portal wraps the most popular ones in clickable buttons, for whenever typing commands still feels like a hurdle.

tips.title: If your app menu or system theme briefly looks like plain Fedora instead of Bazzite's own branding, that's a known cosmetic quirk on some setups, not a sign the install went wrong.
tips.body: It's purely visual and doesn't affect how the system works.

tips.title: Systemd services come in two flavors, and the difference matters.
tips.body: A user service only runs while you're logged in. A system service runs regardless, and needs elevated permissions to set up. Linger is the setting that bridges the gap: enabling it for your user, a one-time command, tells the system to keep your own services running around the clock even with no active login session, which is what you almost always want for something like a media or file server.

tips.title: Distrobox is your escape hatch for traditional dev environments.
tips.body: It runs a full, unrestricted container of nearly any Linux distro side by side with Bazzite, useful when a tool or library genuinely needs a traditional package manager rather than Flatpak or layering.

tips.title: Some tools default to ignoring your GPU, especially the integrated one.
tips.body: Local AI and GPU-accelerated tools sometimes need an explicit environment variable or config flag before they'll actually use hardware acceleration, particularly integrated graphics. If something feels slower than it should, check whether the tool is actually seeing your GPU before assuming your hardware is the limit.

tips.title: Installers that assume a writable slash usr can silently fail on Bazzite.
tips.body: Because the base filesystem is read-only, some traditional installer scripts, especially ones that try to create system users or write to slash usr directly, fail quietly instead of erroring clearly. If a service isn't starting after what looked like a successful install, that's a common cause worth checking first.

tips.title: AppImage is a fourth way software sometimes comes packaged, alongside Flatpak, layering, and containers.
tips.body: It's a single self-contained file that runs without installing anything system-wide, handy for the occasional app that hasn't published a Flatpak yet.

tips.title: DaVinci Resolve's Linux audio gap isn't fixed by paying for Studio.
tips.body: The missing AAC audio decode affects both the free and paid versions on Linux, it's a licensing issue, not a feature gate. Most phone and camera footage uses AAC audio, so it's worth knowing before an import goes silent.

tips.title: Codecs decide more than feature lists do.
tips.body: When comparing editors, check what audio and video formats they can actually decode before comparing timelines and effects. An editor that routes through the system's own ffmpeg, like Kdenlive does on Bazzite, tends to just work with real-world footage with no conversion step.

tips.title: There's no single perfect photo editor, but there's a solid default.
tips.body: GIMP with the community PhotoGIMP preset is the most purpose-built free option for general editing, reshaping the interface to feel more familiar. Darktable handles RAW processing as a separate, complementary tool rather than a competing all-in-one.

tips.title: Modern noise reduction tools sound noticeably better than the older style.
tips.body: Older spectral subtraction noise reduction can make voice audio sound muffled or underwater. Look for a modern, speech-aware option, Kdenlive's Arndn effect is one, rather than defaulting to whichever noise reduction effect appears first in the list.

tips.title: A local tool won't load at localhost? Try 127.0.0.1 instead.
tips.body: Brave has a known bug where the literal word localhost fails to load local web-based tools due to its HTTPS-upgrade behavior. Swapping in 127.0.0.1 with the same port loads it instantly, a quick fix for anyone running local creative or AI tools with a web interface.

tips.title: Ignore Proton until something breaks.
tips.body: Steam handles the vast majority of games automatically through Proton, Valve's built-in compatibility layer. You don't need to configure anything up front.

tips.title: If a game misbehaves, work through compatibility options in order.
tips.body: Try the stable, default Proton version first, then Proton Experimental, Valve's own newer rolling branch, and only reach for GE-Proton, a community-enhanced version with extra patches, as the last resort for the specific games that need it.

tips.title: Most major game controllers work right out of the box.
tips.body: Xbox, PlayStation, Switch, and most third-party controllers are supported without extra setup or driver hunting.

tips.title: Check ProtonDB before assuming a game won't run.
tips.body: It's a community-maintained compatibility database for exactly this question, worth a quick look before spending time troubleshooting something that's already a known issue, or already confirmed to run great.

tips.title: Steam Gaming Mode is an optional console-style layer, not something everyone needs.
tips.body: It's most useful for handhelds and living room setups, a regular desktop install works perfectly well without ever touching it.

tips.title: If a Windows game insists your Linux graphics drivers are out of date, it's almost always a false alarm.
tips.body: Driver version numbers are named differently between Windows and Linux, so a game checking for a specific Windows-style number will flag a perfectly current Linux driver as outdated. Safe to ignore.

tips.title: Changing your Proton compatibility version too often can temporarily lock you out of a game.
tips.body: Titles protected by Denuvo anti-tamper treat a Proton version switch like activating the game on new hardware, more than five switches within 24 hours can trigger a temporary lockout until that window passes.

tips.title: If a native Linux version of a game won't launch, try forcing a different compatibility tool anyway.
tips.body: Some native Linux ports actually run better, or only run at all, through Steam's Legacy Runtime compatibility option, found in the game's properties under Compatibility.

tips.title: A common piece of gaming advice you'll see repeated online, adding gamemoderun to a game's launch options, can actually stop it from launching on Bazzite.
tips.body: That optimization tool isn't part of Bazzite by default, so the launch option just fails. Remove it from launch options if a game that used to work suddenly won't start.

tips.title: Keep your Steam game library off NTFS-formatted drives.
tips.body: An external or secondary drive formatted the Windows way can cause permission errors with Steam and Proton, reformatting it to a native Linux filesystem avoids the headache.

tips.title: An Xbox controller stuck in a Bluetooth connecting loop, with the Xbox button endlessly flashing, is usually a firmware problem, not a Bazzite problem.
tips.body: Updating the controller's firmware through Microsoft's official accessories app, which needs a Windows machine or a virtual one, typically clears it right up.

tips.title: If a specific game won't launch and you need help troubleshooting, Steam can generate a diagnostic log for it.
tips.body: Adding a launch option to that one game creates a log file in your home folder that's genuinely useful to share when asking for help.

tips.title: Skip the system-wide Google or Microsoft sign-in.
tips.body: System Settings, then Online Accounts, is a known source of frustration for connecting these logins, the embedded browser window often trips the provider's own security warnings. Add the account directly inside the app that needs it, like the mail or calendar app, instead, it's more reliable.

tips.title: Your default email client isn't your only option, but it's a fine one.
tips.body: KDE's own KMail, part of the Kontact suite and matching your desktop theme automatically, and Betterbird, a polished Thunderbird fork, are both real alternatives if the interface bothers you, but the plain default remains a solid, well-supported choice most people stick with.

tips.title: Pair your email client with a matching calendar app.
tips.body: Merkuro Calendar is KDE's own calendar app, syncing with Google Calendar, Outlook, and CalDAV generally, a natural companion to KMail if you've set that up.

tips.title: Ad blocking without running a server.
tips.body: Point your network DNS at a free public resolver like AdGuard or NextDNS for system-wide blocking, no self-hosting, no maintenance required.

tips.title: The computer you already have can be your NAS.
tips.body: Combining Samba file sharing with Tailscale for remote access gets you phone-to-desktop file access without buying dedicated hardware.

tips.title: Tailscale is useful even if you're not self-hosting anything.
tips.body: It creates a private, secure network between your own devices, letting your phone reach your desktop, or vice versa, without opening anything to the public internet. Once you are self-hosting, it's also the safe way to use those services from away from home, since private remote access never means exposing your machine publicly.

tips.title: A use your Gmail here privacy feature is often mostly IMAP with a label.
tips.body: Some privacy-focused email services let you connect an existing Gmail account, but mail to anyone not also on that service still flows through Google's servers unencrypted, same as before. Worth checking what the feature actually changes technically before assuming it's a bigger privacy win than it is.

tips.title: Homebrew is the tidy way to install command-line tools.
tips.body: Bazzite includes Homebrew, the same package manager many developers know from macOS, and it's the recommended route for terminal and command-line programs. It installs everything into its own isolated area without touching the base system, so nothing it does can destabilize your install.

tips.title: Reach for the tools in a sensible order, from least invasive to most.
tips.body: For a graphical app, try Flatpak first. For a command-line tool, try Homebrew. For anything needing a full traditional Linux environment, use a Distrobox container. Only fall back to layering a package onto the system image as a genuine last resort, since layered packages can hold up future system updates until they're removed.

tips.title: Managing containers doesn't have to mean memorizing commands.
tips.body: Bazzite ships with graphical container managers, BoxBuddy and others, that let you create, enter, and remove Distrobox containers through a normal window with buttons, no command-line ritual required.

tips.title: A layered package can quietly block your next system update.
tips.body: Because layered packages have to be rebuilt against each new system image, one that doesn't cooperate can stall updates entirely until you remove it. If updates suddenly stop applying, a package you layered a while ago is a prime suspect.

tips.title: Quadlet turns a container into a proper background service.
tips.body: When you want something running continuously, a local database, a personal tool, a server, Quadlet lets you define it as a systemd service using a short text file, so it starts on boot and is managed with the same commands as any other service. It's more advanced than the everyday install methods, but it's the clean, native way to run persistent things on Bazzite.

tips.title: VS Code works best when it runs inside your container, not outside it.
tips.body: A common friction point is installing an editor on the base system but keeping your actual tools in a container. Running the editor from inside the same Distrobox container as your toolchain, or using its remote container support, keeps everything lined up and avoids a lot of "works in the terminal but not the editor" confusion.

tips.title: DaVinci Resolve has an official one-command install now.
tips.body: Rather than wrestling with the immutable filesystem, Bazzite provides a ujust install-resolve command that sets Resolve up inside a purpose-built container for you. It's the sanctioned path, and it sidesteps the dependency errors people used to hit trying to install it directly.

tips.title: A sandboxed creative app can't see your files until you let it.
tips.body: Because Flatpak apps are sandboxed, a video editor or audio tool may only have access to a few folders by default, which is why your media sometimes seems invisible to it. The pre-installed Flatseal app lets you grant an app access to the folders it needs through a simple checklist, no terminal required.

tips.title: OBS runs well here, and Bazzite even pre-tunes some of it.
tips.body: OBS Studio, the standard for recording and streaming, works through Flatpak, and Bazzite ships with sensible integrations already in place. It's a genuinely strong platform for a creator, contrary to the assumption that streaming and recording are Windows-only strengths.

tips.title: Your audio runs through PipeWire, which makes routing sound between apps easier, not harder.
tips.body: Bazzite uses PipeWire, a modern audio system that can route audio between applications flexibly, the kind of thing that used to require fiddly extra software on Linux. For a creator, that means sending one app's sound into another, or splitting audio sources, is far more approachable than it once was.

tips.title: Color and RAW work each have a mature free home.
tips.body: Beyond general photo editing, Krita is a genuinely professional painting and digital art tool, and Blender covers 3D, motion graphics, and even video editing in one package. Neither is a compromise pick, both are used in real professional pipelines.

tips.title: Keep large media libraries off the sandbox's default path.
tips.body: Sandboxed creative apps behave best when your big project and media folders are in a location you've explicitly granted access to, rather than scattered in spots the sandbox blocks. Deciding on one media folder and granting access to it once saves repeated "file not found" frustration later.

tips.title: Bazaar is your app store, and it's the right first stop for almost anything.
tips.body: Bazzite includes Bazaar, a friendly graphical store for browsing and installing apps, no command line involved. For the large majority of everyday software, this is the intended and easiest way to get it, think of it the way you'd think of an app store on your phone.

tips.title: LibreOffice opens and saves your Office files, and Bazzite smooths its rough edges.
tips.body: The pre-installed LibreOffice suite handles Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files, and Bazzite grants it the extra permissions it needs to print and integrate with the desktop properly, something that occasionally trips up office software on other setups.

tips.title: Your apps live in a few different places, and one command updates almost all of them.
tips.body: On this kind of system, software arrives through a few separate channels: the app store for most graphical apps, containers for services, Homebrew for command-line tools, and the occasional standalone file. It sounds like a lot, but a single command, ujust update, sweeps through nearly all of them at once and keeps everything current. You don't have to track them individually.

tips.title: Android apps can run on your desktop if you need them.
tips.body: Through a tool called Waydroid, Bazzite can run Android apps in a window, useful for the occasional app that only exists on mobile. It's not something most people need day to day, but it's there when a specific app leaves you no other option.

tips.title: Your files live in familiar, ordinary folders.
tips.body: Documents, Downloads, Pictures, and the rest work exactly as you'd expect, in a normal home folder you own and control. The immutable, protected part of Bazzite is the operating system itself, not your personal files, which stay fully yours to organize however you like.

tips.title: Let the app store handle updates rather than chasing them per app.
tips.body: Because most of your software comes from one place, you rarely need to hunt down individual updaters the way you might have on Windows. Checking the store now and then, or running the one update command, keeps everything current without the per-app nagging.

tips.title: Your computer can quietly run real services in the background with Quadlet.
tips.body: Want your own media server, file sync, or ad-blocker running at home? Quadlet lets you define each as a background service from a short text file, so it starts automatically and stays running. It's the clean, built-in way to self-host on Bazzite without bolting on extra platforms.

tips.title: Rootless containers are a real privacy and safety win.
tips.body: Bazzite is built to run containers "rootless," meaning a self-hosted service runs with limited privileges rather than full control of your system. If something in a container were ever compromised, that boundary sharply limits the damage, a meaningful safety margin when you're hosting things yourself.

tips.title: You don't have to manage self-hosted services from the command line.
tips.body: Web-based dashboards like Cockpit or Portainer give you a browser window to start, stop, and monitor your containers and services, turning self-hosting from a terminal chore into something closer to a control panel.

tips.title: Popular self-hosted apps are mostly a matter of pointing to the right container image.
tips.body: The bulk of the self-hosting world, media servers, file sync, note-taking, dashboards, is distributed as ready-made container images. On Bazzite that means running one is usually a matter of referencing the image and setting a folder and a port, not building anything from scratch.

tips.title: Keep a self-hosted service's data in a folder you chose on purpose.
tips.body: Point each service's storage at a clear, deliberate location in your home folder rather than leaving it buried in container internals. It makes backing up your data trivial and keeps everything easy to find later.

tips.title: Self-hosting on Bazzite doesn't mean turning your machine into a fragile server.
tips.body: Because services run as isolated containers on top of the stable, protected base system, experimenting with them doesn't put your actual computer at risk. If a service misbehaves, you remove its container and the rest of your system is untouched.

tips.title: Your computer can be a private media server, no subscription, no account.
tips.body: A free program called Jellyfin turns a folder of movies and shows into a proper library, with artwork and descriptions, streamed to your TV and phone over your own network. It's the same idea as a photo server like Immich, but for video, and unlike the big commercial options there's no account, no monthly fee, and nothing phoning home.

tips.title: Ripping your own discs takes two free tools that work together.
tips.body: MakeMKV pulls the movie off a Blu-ray or DVD you own into a file, and HandBrake shrinks that file down to a sensible size without an obvious quality loss. Both install from the app store as Flatpaks. The usual workflow is rip with the first, compress with the second, then drop the result into your Jellyfin library.

tips.title: A disc drive needs a special permission before ripping software can see it properly.
tips.body: Because of how Linux isolates hardware, MakeMKV can fail to read a disc even when the drive is clearly connected and the disc mounts fine in your file manager. The fix is a one-time udev rule granting raw access to the optical drive. It's a known step, not a sign anything is broken, and once it's in place disc reading just works.

tips.title: Most external Blu-ray drives are the same drive inside a different shell.
tips.body: A large share of external drives, including several well-known brands, are rebadged versions of the same underlying mechanism from one manufacturer. If you specifically want to avoid that manufacturer, Pioneer is the genuinely different option, at a somewhat higher price. Worth knowing before you assume two differently branded drives are actually different hardware.

tips.title: Direct play is what you want, and it's why hardware video acceleration matters.
tips.body: When your TV app can play a video file exactly as it's stored, that's direct play, smooth and effortless. When it can't, the server has to convert the video on the fly, which is heavy work. Turning on your machine's built-in hardware video acceleration, the same VAAPI setup that speeds up a photo server, makes those conversions painless on the occasions they do happen.

tips.title: Ripping a disc you own still sits in a legal gray area in the US.
tips.body: Even for a disc you paid for, breaking its copy protection to rip it bumps into anti-circumvention rules regardless of ownership. It's extremely widely done, and this isn't legal advice, but it's more honest to know that going in than to find out later.

tips.title: The best TV box for a private server is a plain Android TV device.
tips.body: A media streamer like an Nvidia Shield, or most Android TV or Google TV boxes, runs the free Jellyfin app and plays your library directly. You point it at your own server over your home network, nothing leaves the house, and you're not renting anything.

tips.title: A streaming box can be quieted down without replacing it.
tips.body: Devices like the Nvidia Shield collect more than they need to by default, but swapping the home screen for a free launcher like Projectivy, deleting the advertising ID, and pointing the device at your ad-blocking DNS strips out most of the noise without buying new hardware.

tips.title: Standalone app files have a helper that makes them behave like real installed apps.
tips.body: An AppImage is a single self-contained file you can run from anywhere, handy for the occasional app that isn't in the store, but on its own it won't show up in your menu or update itself. A free tool called GearLever fixes both, giving the app a proper menu entry and handling its updates, so a loose file starts acting like a first-class citizen.

tips.title: If an AMD mini PC feels starved for memory, check one BIOS setting.
tips.body: Some AMD machines reserve a large fixed chunk of memory for graphics by default, which can leave the actual system with far less than you paid for and make everything feel sluggish. The setting is in the BIOS under the graphics configuration, often called UMA Frame Buffer Size. Lowering it can hand a surprising amount of memory back to the system, worth checking on any AMD APU machine that feels slower than its specs suggest.

tips.title: There's no single manage all my apps window, and that's the normal trade, not a flaw.
tips.body: Because software lives in a few different places, no one screen lists every app with an update button. The app store covers most of it, GearLever covers standalone files, and the update command covers the rest. It's slightly more spread out than a Mac, in exchange for a base system that's very hard to break.

tips.title: A background container needs the full image address, not the short name.
tips.body: When you define a container service, naming the image as just a short name often fails, because the tooling wants the complete address including the registry it comes from. If a service refuses to start and the image name looks too short, that's a common cause, and prefixing it with the full registry path usually fixes it immediately.

tips.title: Shared folders for a container often need a specific flag here, or they get blocked.
tips.body: The security layer, SELinux, can silently prevent a container from reading a folder you mounted into it, which looks like the app is broken when it's really just being denied access. Adding the relabel flag to the mount, a small Z on the volume line, tells the system to allow it. It's one of the most common invisible walls people hit when self-hosting on Bazzite.

tips.title: Your containers can update themselves on a schedule.
tips.body: Beyond updating apps by hand, you can enable a built-in timer that periodically checks your running containers for new versions and updates them automatically. Turn it on once and your self-hosted services quietly stay current without you thinking about it.

tips.title: Track updates for any app you depend on using its releases feed.
tips.body: Every project on GitHub publishes a feed of its releases. Drop that feed address into a feed reader, a self-hosted one like FreshRSS works well, and you'll find out the day a new version of something you rely on ships, without checking any page by hand. Especially useful for community-built apps that update irregularly.

tips.title: You can run your own private search engine.
tips.body: A tool called SearXNG runs on your own machine and fetches results from many search engines at once, stripping out the tracking along the way, so your searches aren't tied back to you by any single provider. You can point your browser at it, and it can even feed local AI tools that need to look things up.

tips.title: A private photo library at home can fully replace the cloud kind.
tips.body: Immich is a self-hosted photo and video app that looks and feels like the big cloud photo services, with phone backup, albums, search, and face grouping, but every photo stays on hardware you own. For a lot of people it's the single most satisfying thing to self-host, because it directly replaces a service they were paying for and being tracked by.

tips.title: There's a real, if unofficial, way to run the Affinity apps here.
tips.body: Affinity's design apps, a popular affordable alternative to the big subscription design suite, have no official Linux version, but the community maintains a packaged build that runs them through a compatibility layer, distributed as a single downloadable file. It genuinely works, and it opens your existing Affinity files.

tips.title: If you rely on that Affinity build, export your files to open formats early.
tips.body: Because it's a volunteer-maintained, unofficial build, a future update to the app could break it, and then your files would be stranded in a format nothing else opens well. The safe move is to open your existing work and export it to open formats in one sitting, SVG for vector, layered PSD or TIFF for image work, PDF for layouts, so a broken build later is an annoyance rather than a loss. It's the same own your files thinking that applies to everything else.

tips.title: For a quick Photoshop-like editor with no install, a browser tab does the job.
tips.body: Photopea is a free, browser-based image editor with a genuinely familiar interface, and it opens layered PSD files directly. For a lot of quick edits it removes the need to install anything at all, and it works the same on any machine you sit down at.

lookup.note: The safe default, familiar and reliable, works immediately.
KDE-native, syncs with Google and Outlook directly.
Codecs just work, no silent-audio surprises on import.
PhotoGIMP reshapes the interface to feel familiar, Darktable handles RAW separately.
Free, private, and syncs entirely on your own terms.
Free and offline, Microsoft 365's own web apps also work fine in-browser if compatibility matters more than offline use.
